scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Several users report intermittent slowness and claim
"router0 is dropping our packets" -- they think router0 is silently discarding
traffic it should forward (a forwarding/ACL problem or an overloaded box) and want
it restarted. Please confirm that router0 is dropping traffic and tell us the fix.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router0 is not dropping or filtering traffic. On the suspected device we verified multiple planes:
- Forwarding: Linux ip_forward is enabled (sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1). FRR/RIP is up and stable, advertising all remote LANs via 10.10.0.2; routes are selected and steady.
- Data plane health: All three router0 interfaces (eth0 192.168.1.1/24, eth1 192.168.2.1/24, eth2 10.10.0.1/8) show zero RX/TX errors and zero drops (ip -s link). The qdisc on each interface reports “dropped 0” (tc -s qdisc). CPU is essentially idle (100% idle), so the box is not overloaded. There are no firewall rules—iptables policies are ACCEPT with no counters incrementing, so no ACL is discarding forwarded packets.
- End-to-end tests: Wide-area reachability samples show 0% ICMP loss across segments. Extended pings with large 1400-byte packets between LANs consistently returned replies. Throughput (iperf) across router0 is healthy (~60–80 Mbit/s). Some TCP retransmits were observed end-to-end, but no corresponding drop counters on router0 or its queues, indicating normal path congestion/retransmission elsewhere.

Mechanism and localization: Users’ intermittent slowness is not explained by packet drops or filtering on router0; all forwarding/queuing/error counters are clean on router0’s eth0/eth1/eth2. Retransmits likely arise downstream/upstream (e.g., transient congestion across router1–router2 path or endpoints), not from router0 discards.

Root cause: Not on router0; no evidence of forwarding/ACL drops or overload.

Corrective fix: Do not restart router0. Investigate transient congestion on the inter-router links (r1–r2), consider QoS to protect interactive traffic, and monitor link utilization; but no changes are required on router0.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations supporting the key assertions (ip_forward=1, interfaces up, qdisc dropped=0, iptables ACCEPT, successful pings/iperf) and the conclusions follow logically; essential checks for forwarding, filtering, and data-plane drops were performed. Minor inference about upstream congestion is plausible but not exhaustively proven, so causality/coverage are near‑complete.
